The present Appeal No. 334 of 2017 has been filed by Assam Power Distribution Company Limited under Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 challenging the Corrigendum order dated 03.05.2017 **(Impugned Order)** read with order dated 30.03.2017 passed by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission in Petition No. 129/GT/2015. Brief facts of the case, relevant for disposal of the present Appeal are summarized hereunder : ONGC, however, no material has been placed on record either before the Central Commission or this Tribunal 28. It is to further state that this Tribunal neither exercise jurisdiction over ONGC’s internal commercial and management decisions nor ONGC is a party in the present proceedings, we shall therefore limit our deliberations with regard to provisions of GSPA executed between OTPC, the respondent, and ONGC. 29. The learned Counsel on behalf of Respondent No.1- OTPC has contended that Appellant confined its case on one contention that ONGC being shareholder of OTPC could have ensured adequate supply and relied upon the letter dated 18.12.2015 issued by OTPC to CEA to allege that gas was diverted to Monarchak project. Though the said letter was submitted along with the Appeal, however, it was not placed before the commission when reply was filed by Appellant to them on 12.02.2016. With regard to admissibility of such document at Appellant stage, without an application and with no specific order by this Tribunal, it has been submitted that it cannot form part of the evidentiary record for examining the correctness of the Impugned Order and there is procedural bar under Order XLI Rule 27 of CPC 1908. 30. In this context, it is noted that Respondent No.1-OTPC, in its reply dated 03.04.2018 before this Tribunal has referred to the same letter dated 18.12.2015 to submit that OTPC has actively pursued with CEA apprising them about the shortage of gas supply at its Palatana Project and respondent has not placed any evidence that it had, at any stage, questioned the admissibility of such document at Appellate Stage. It is well settled that proceedings before this Tribunal are governed by the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Regulations framed thereunder. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), in its strict sense, does not apply to proceedings before this Tribunal. While principles of natural justice and certain procedural safeguards embodied in the CPC may be invoked for guidance, the rigours of the CPC cannot be imported at a belated stage of appellate adjudication. In the present matter, the Respondent has sought to raise objections regarding the admissibility of a document on the ground that it was not filed before the State Commission, particularly at a stage when the Appeal is being finally heard in later part of year 2025, is untenable. The Tribunal, exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 111 of the Electricity Act, is not bound by the technicalities of the CPC. The Tribunal is empowered to examine the correctness of the Impugned Order on the basis of the material placed before it, and once both parties have themselves relied upon the document in question, the objection to its admissibility loses all force. Accordingly, this Tribunal holds that the provisions of the CPC cannot be pressed into service at such a belated stage to defeat substantive justice. The objection raised by the Respondent is, therefore, rejected. - _(ii) any other breach by the Seller of its obligations in accordance with this Agreement.”_ - _(b) The Party asserting the claim of Force Majeure shall have the burden of proving the circumstances constitute valid grounds of Force Majeure under_ _this clause and that such Party has exercised reasonable diligence and efforts to remedy the cause of any alleged Force Majeure.”_ vide letter dated 17.08.2016 & 31.10.2016, and noting that relief being sought by Appellant (NEEPCO) could have been claimed under the GSPA and directed against the gas supplier, however taking cognizance of the direction of central govt, vis-à-vis obligations of gas supplier to supply as per that, resulted in reduction of supply for the Appellant Project. Since Central commission has not examined the issue in this perspective, this Tribunal without expressing any opinion on the merit of the case, remanded the matter to Central commission for fresh consideration from that perspective. In our view, this judgement cannot be construed to be holding that arranging fuel is not the responsibility of generator and it is entitled to relaxation in NAPAF in case of shortage of supply. The shortage in supply of gas for the subject project in the referred judgement was considering the directives of Govt, while no such Govt directive have been referred in the present case, which mandates ONGC to divert the supply elsewhere. Thus, the facts in the present case are different than the case referred and accordingly reliance placed on this judgement by Respondent is of no avail. We further observe that the Respondent has sought to place reliance upon the order passed by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) pursuant to the remand directions issued by this Tribunal in the aforesaid matter. In our considered view, such reliance is misplaced. This Tribunal, being a statutory appellate forum, is bound by the pronouncements of superior judicial fora and not by the orders of the regulatory commission, which is subordinate in the judicial hierarchy. While the orders of the Commission may provide administrative context or factual narration, they do not constitute binding precedent upon this Tribunal. The jurisprudential discipline requires us to follow the ratio laid down by higher courts, and not to be guided by regulatory directions issued in the course of remand proceedings. Accordingly, the order passed by the CERC upon remand cannot be treated as determinative for the present adjudication and does not need consideration by us.
